posts:
Richmond DPU celebrated a seamless billing system launch while internal emails showed dozens of error messages piling up.
Evidence: 80 error msgs at 10 AM, FOIA fees
#Aletheia #Richmond #Utilities

Officials claimed an abundance of testing and a successful rollout of new customer account systems.
Stated Judgement: (+1.0, +1.0) — Greater Good

Internal emails revealed immediate data glitches, missing meter reads, and broken PromisePay accounts while public PR spun success.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.55, -0.75) — Lesser Evil

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception.
Spinning a flawless rollout while internal systems throw error codes erodes public trust in municipal administration.
Integrity: Meaningful Distortion (Hypocrisy: 4.1, z: 2)

- Richmond DPU: FAIL (-0.6, -0.8) — Public spin masked internal data chaos.
- The Richmonder: PASS (0.8, 0.5) — Uncovered reality via FOIA reporting.
On May 26, 2026, Richmond's DPU announced a successful billing system launch. Simultaneously, internal emails showed senior staff flooded with error messages and broken customer records.

The Bright Side:
Investigative reporting and FOIA requests successfully punctured municipal PR spin to expose operational realities.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing WHAT was claimed (flawless software deployment) with WHO bore the cost (residents facing billing errors).

Social Physics Analysis:
City officials ran a Smart Selfish Maneuver by issuing upbeat press releases to shield leadership, leaving customer service agents and residents to absorb the fallout of broken data links.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When institutional self-preservation overrides operational transparency, administrative friction metastasizes into public distrust.

The Unavoidable Truth: Complex municipal software transitions require transparent acknowledgment of friction rather than PR gloss.

The Unavoidable Lie: Eighty error messages received by 10 AM equates to a successful rollout.

Emails: Amid public celebration, data glitches were piling up during DPU billing system transition

The data issues were causing several problems, according to internal emails obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request.

Actual Article Body:
Completing registration...

Success! Check your inbox for our email.

On the morning of May 26, Richmond’s Department of Public Utilities announced it had successfully launched two new systems meant to track customer accounts and improve service in the field.

An “abundance of testing, training, dress rehearsals and validations” had laid the groundwork for a successful rollout, DPU said, but officials would continue to watch for issues that might impact customers.

Around the same time that news release went out at 10 a.m., DPU Senior Deputy Director Jamie Porter noticed some problems.

“Team,” Porter wrote in a 9:53 a.m. email. “I am getting error messages from Kubra.”

A data connection between the KUBRA payment platform and DPU’s new Oracle Customer Cloud Service, which held customer account info, seemed off. A data integration process called “CCSKubra_GetBill” was repeatedly throwing up error notifications.

“I’ve received about 80 of these emails,” Porter wrote seven minutes later, just as DPU’s celebratory news release was going out.

The data issues were causing several problems, according to internal emails obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request. The FOIA request sought records between May 26, the day DPU announced it had successfully launched the new system, and June 1, the first time DPU sent a news release acknowledging there’d been a “system glitch.”

Customer service agents were unable to pull up bill information in the new system, and couldn’t schedule service appointments. Some service orders weren’t going through at all.

“Until these issues are resolved; to have documentation of the issue and the customer's needs, we are submitting tickets,” wrote contractor Tiffany Blackaby.

There also seemed to be issues with meter read data coming in from the field.

“I imported the file. The main route is only showing 588 meters. Last month there were 8515 meters,” DPU business systems specialist Sherri Porter wrote on May 26.

The problems seemed particularly serious for data involving PromisePay plans, which allow customers to pay off past due balances by splitting them up into monthly installments.

According to the emails, some PromisePay accounts were showing no balances, no service address or no due dates. In data terms, those fields were “null.”

“I wanted to check in again on the null due dates: Instead of leaving them as null, can we please set the due date to the next date a bill will be issued?” wrote a contractor for the PromisePay vendor.

At one point, more than 1,000 accounts were showing up with a null service address.

At least one account was showing late charges, which isn’t supposed to happen with PromisePay customers who are trying to get caught up. That forced the programming team to try to find a fix in the Oracle system to detach late charges from PromisePay accounts.

On June 1, there seemed to be confusion about which aspects of the system were going live when.

A DPU employee informed the Kubra team the city wasn’t receiving some payments through its online billing platforms because the systems weren’t connecting right.

“We were receiving transactions from your test system to our production prior to go live,” wrote DPU’s Max Pop. “Would you kindly have a look and see if you are attempting to send us transactions.”

Faisal Alvi, a senior project manager at KUBRA, indicated the connection at issue wasn’t up and running yet.

“It is part of the MyHQ/EZPAY changes that will Go live at a later date,” Alvi wrote.

Some staffers seemed to have trouble using the live customer system instead of the test version. One email sought help for someone whose system kept going back to the testing status.

“Can you assist or advise what she needs to do to get in the production screen,” a DPU customer care specialist wrote. “She has reset her password, log out the system and logged back in. I[t] goes back to test.”
